baseline_requirements: Incorporate the corporate colour and slogan in the design; ignore teletext and everything except TV control.
The remote must look and feel stylish/fancy (top consumer priority), not merely functional.
The design must be innovative with cutting-edge technology, without adding unnecessary functional features; innovation should contribute to look and feel (e.g. lighting up when picked up).
The remote must be easy to use and user friendly throughout while still having technology.
Use soft, spongy, ergonomic, friendly-to-handle materials to capitalise on this year's trend.
Use a unifying theme (marketing identity, e.g. lemon/lime fruit series tied to the yellow company colour) across shape, materials and series.
Lighting feature: buttons that light up (backlit, possibly in different colours) when touched or picked up, usable in the dark, adding a high-tech feel.
Consider interchangeable covers for the control.
The standby button should be red.
Buttons should be large, easy and comfortable to press.
Volume up and down buttons must be clearly distinguishable from each other.
If the corporate colour scheme allows, use a very bright colour so the control is easy to find, avoiding tackiness.
Avoid the big square block look; the control should be comfortable to hold, small and slim but not too small to use.
Extra features beyond the basics should be hidden and only reachable with special effort, e.g. opening a cover.
If voice activation is included, a button alternative must always be provided.
Consider voice control that talks back to confirm user actions.
Power the remote with a hybrid system: a battery combined with a secondary source (kinetic as main idea, battery as backup).
Use as few and as simple components as possible to reduce cost, time to market and development complexity.
Include a really good battery so users do not have to charge the remote every few days.
Consider a kinetic mechanism, like an automatic watch, to power or trigger the light when the remote is picked up.
Very curvy shape with fruit-like texture and colour, but not literally a fruit shape.
Use a mix of plastic and rubber with curved shapes for a warmer, more comfortable feel, instead of boxy materials like wood or titanium; consider textured soft-feel plastic.
The remote should fold up to reveal a third group of controls inside, with volume controls on the body.
Colour scheme must include yellow somewhere, e.g. yellow background with bold-coloured buttons.
Use a slightly transparent yellow-tinted case with one or two subtle low-power lights so it glows softly in the dark.
Include a way to skip many channels at once (number buttons), since a jog dial is slow for about fifty channels.
Include the company slogan on the remote design (suggested on the side of the casing).
Add a jog dial positioned to fit the shape of the remote.
Incorporate a logo into the design.
Explore a flat, spun jog dial rather than a protruding one.
baseline_decisions: Target user group is 15 to 35 year olds (decided in the previous meeting).
The remote will use non-rechargeable batteries (decided in the previous meeting).
Presentations go in order (Andrew, Craig, David), with discussion at the end and decisions afterward.
Only basic functions are visible on the remote; the rest are hidden (advanced functions go inside the folding section, basic on the front).
The remote will have a snowman shape: larger body in the hand and a smaller bubble at the top for other functions.
No LCD display and no talk-back (speaker output) feature in the remote.
The design will use rubber buttons.
The team agreed to incorporate a jog dial, with no one opposing.
Jog dial design details are left to the designers to discuss among themselves.
Materials are plastic and rubber, as previously discussed.
This meeting must end with a decision on the product concepts; time is limited (about fifteen minutes, later about five minutes remaining).
The corporate colour appears to be yellow (from website and bottom band); not confirmed.
Design trade-offs are driven by cost, complexity and device size; more physical components mean higher cost and power use.
The case can be flat or curved; available materials are probably not combinable, but this is unconfirmed with the supplier.
Material limits: rubber case restricts power options (solar panel); titanium cannot be curved and must be square; wood cannot be curved; plastic has no restrictions.
Complex UI features such as an LCD panel and scroll wheel require more complicated logic chips; standard buttons do not.
Solar power is a poor fit for Europe or countries with seasons, so it cannot be the only power source.
The next meeting takes place in thirty minutes.
